payload.claim: In a backtest of four SPY allocation approaches over January 2000–August 2025, the approach that produced the lowest drawdown also produced a lower growth-of-$1 outcome than a fully-invested (buy-and-hold) SPY approach.
payload.quote:
The growth of $1 across four SPY allocation approaches, January 2000–August 2025. All four lines come from the historical backtest discussed in the article.
I wanted to know how much difference a simple, mechanical change in equity exposure would have made over a full cycle. I tested four portfolio rules on more than 25 years of daily SPY data. The lowest-drawdown approach cushioned the worst losses, but an investor who followed it ended up with less money than someone who stayed fully invested. The trade-off is substantial enough to deserve a close look.

data_required: SPY daily price data, January 2000 to August 2025
testability.notes: Exact rules defining the four approaches are not specified in this excerpt, limiting full reproducibility, but the sample window, instrument, and core result (lowest-drawdown underperforms buy-and-hold) are stated.

payload.claim: Using recent price volatility and a longer-term market trend measure individually, and then combined, to adjust SPY equity exposure produces different outcomes in the backtest, with volatility reacting quickly to shocks and the trend measure capturing slower deterioration.
payload.quote: The exercise begins with two familiar pieces of information: recent price volatility and the longer-term market trend. Volatility can rise quickly during a shock; a trend measure can pick up a slower deterioration. I tested what each contributes, then what happens when the two are used together.

source.title: Can You Reduce Risk Without Missing the Rally?

testability.notes: No specific parameter values (lookback windows, thresholds) are given in this passage, reducing precision; the claim is stated at the generality the quote supports.

payload.claim: Executing the same order (holding participation rate and order size constant) in the final hour of the trading session is consistently less costly than executing it earlier in the day.
payload.quote: The findings indicate that executing the same order in the final hour of the trading session is consistently less costly than executing it earlier in the day.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

payload.claim: For Russell 2000 constituent stocks, simulating trades of 1% of daily volume at a fixed 15% participation rate using TAQ data shows that trading costs decline substantially as the session progresses, with the lowest market impact observed in the final two hours of the trading day.
payload.quote: To quantify this effect we used Trade and Quote (TAQ) data to simulate trading 1% of daily volume in Russell 2000 constituent stocks at a fixed 15% participation rate. Figure 1 illustrates this effect, highlighting distinct cost profiles throughout the day. The analysis reveals that trading costs decline substantially as the session progresses, with the lowest market impact observed in the final two hours.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

payload.claim: Time of day exerts an independent and significant influence on execution cost beyond participation rate, and intraday volume does not fully explain where and when liquidity is cheapest.
payload.quote: These results suggest that participation rate alone does not determine execution cost. Time of day exerts an independent and significant influence. While most execution algorithms use intraday volume as a proxy for liquidity, the data shows that volume does not fully explain where and when liquidity is cheapest.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

testability.notes: Qualitative interpretive claim derived from the TAQ simulation results described elsewhere in the document.

payload.claim: An analysis of approximately 635,000 live parent orders over four years of trading (excluding canceled and passive limit orders) comparing full-day orders to those initiated in the final hour of the session corroborates the finding that final-hour execution has lower cost.
payload.quote: To validate these results with live execution data, we analyzed approximately 635,000 parent orders from four years of trading, excluding canceled and passive limit orders. We compared full-day orders with those initiated in the final hour of the session and it corroborates the TAQ-based findings, in striking fashion.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

payload.claim: A finite mixture normal regression applied to more than 172,000 firm-year observations spanning 1963 to 2022 reveals latent group structure in the asset growth-return relation.
payload.quote: Using data on more than 172,000 firm-year observations from 1963 to 2022, they let the model find its own structure.

source.title: What Really Drives the Asset Growth Anomaly? New Evidence Points to Mispricing, Not Risk

data_required: firm-year asset growth and return panel 1963-2022
testability.notes: Testable via replication of FMNR methodology, though technique is complex.

payload.claim: A two-latent-group finite mixture normal regression model of the asset growth-return relation fits firm-year return data decisively better than a single-group model, with BIC declining by more than 10,000 when moving from one to two groups.
payload.quote: The result: the data clearly prefer two latent groups over one. Model fit — measured by log-likelihood, Akaike Information Criterion (a simple score that helps you pick the best model from a set of candidates by balancing how well the model fits the data against how complicated the model is), and Bayesian Information Criterion (similar in spirit to AIC but with a stronger penalty for complexity, especially when you have a lot of data) — improves dramatically when moving from a single group to two groups, with the BIC declining by more than 10,000, far past the threshold that constitutes decisive statistical evidence for the more complex model.

source.title: What Really Drives the Asset Growth Anomaly? New Evidence Points to Mispricing, Not Risk

data_required: firm-year asset growth and return panel 1963-2022

payload.claim: In one latent subgroup of firms, next-year returns are highest in the most extreme asset-shrinkage and asset-growth quintiles and lowest in the middle (U-shaped), while in a second latent subgroup returns are lowest at the extremes and least negative in the middle (inverted U-shaped).
payload.quote: In the first latent group, the relation between asset growth and next-year returns is clearly U-shaped: returns are highest for the most extreme asset-shrinkage and asset-growth quintiles, and lowest in the middle. In the second latent group, the pattern flips into an inverted U: returns are lowest at the extremes and least negative in the middle.

source.locator: What the Two Groups Look Like section
source.title: What Really Drives the Asset Growth Anomaly? New Evidence Points to Mispricing, Not Risk

payload.claim: In both the U-shaped and inverted-U-shaped latent return groups, the downward-sloping segment of the asset growth-return relation is steeper than the upward-sloping segment, and this asymmetry generates the net negative asset growth-return relation observed in the overall sample.
payload.quote: Critically, in both groups, the pattern is asymmetric. The downward-sloping segment is steeper than the upward-sloping segment in both the U-shaped and inverted U-shaped groups. That asymmetry is what generates a net negative asset growth-return relation overall — the familiar anomaly — even though the underlying relation within each group is nonlinear rather than a simple downward slope.

payload.quote:
Run the whole sample through a standard single-group
regression
(the way most of the existing literature does it) and you get exactly the well-known monotonic decline in returns across asset growth quintiles. The nonlinearity and the two-regime structure are invisible unless you go looking for them.

payload.quote:
Risk adjustment.
They strip out each firm’s exposure to 10 established risk factors — including CMA itself, along with momentum and four factors explicitly built to capture mispricing and behavioral effects. If the pattern were really compensation for risk, this adjustment should make it disappear. It doesn’t: the U-shaped and inverted U-shaped patterns, and their asymmetry, survive largely intact.

Price-to-value validation.
Using the same price-to-value estimates from their earlier analysis, they show that firms with higher price-to-value ratios (more likely overvalued) are significantly more likely to be assigned by the model to the inverted-U group — exactly what the mispricing story predicts, and a useful external check on whether the statistically-identified groups actually correspond to over- and under-valued firms.

payload.text:
crypto-grid-record-v1: The record of which crypto cells are searched, fixed before any result from them exists. A cell is one asset at one timeframe. This note fixes the whole grid of crypto cells now, in three phases, so that nothing is added to it after results begin to arrive. It changes no existing verdict, moves no strategy, and re-judges nothing on the chain. Until this entry the crypto class was searched as one pooled two-asset book, BTCUSD and ETHUSD together at 1d, one spec per sweep combination. From this entry crypto is searched cell by cell, one single-asset spec per sweep combination, per active cell, as every other asset class already is.

THE ADMISSION LINE. A crypto asset is admitted only if its first daily bar falls on or before 2022-12-31, which is at least 365 days of history before the 2023-12-31 screen cutoff. The line was set by Coen on 2026-10-17, before any result from these cells exists, and applies to every asset alike. 76 declared assets meet it. 24 do not, and none of the 24 is a cell in any phase.

THE GRID.

Phase 1 cells (active from this entry): timeframe 1d on assets: BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, BNBUSDT, XRPUSDT, SOLUSDT, TRXUSDT, ZECUSDT, DOGEUSDT, LINKUSDT, ADAUSDT, XLMUSDT, BCHUSDT, LTCUSDT, HBARUSDT, AVAXUSDT, SHIBUSDT, UNIUSDT, NEARUSDT, PAXGUSDT, AAVEUSDT, DOTUSDT, ICPUSDT, ETCUSDT, QNTUSDT, NEXOUSDT, ALGOUSDT, ATOMUSDT, JSTUSDT, VETUSDT, FILUSDT, CAKEUSDT, INJUSDT, STXUSDT, DASHUSDT, CRVUSDT, APTUSDT, FETUSDT, SUNUSDT, GNOUSDT, LDOUSDT, LUNCUSDT, XTZUSDT, ENSUSDT, CFXUSDT, DCRUSDT, JASMYUSDT, RAYUSDT, CVXUSDT, OPUSDT, IOTAUSDT, COMPUSDT, TWTUSDT, GRTUSDT, THETAUSDT, RUNEUSDT, AXSUSDT, NEOUSDT, CHZUSDT, MANAUSDT, APEUSDT, XECUSDT, ARUSDT, SFPUSDT, SNXUSDT, 1INCHUSDT, SANDUSDT, IMXUSDT, EGLDUSDT, BATUSDT, DYDXUSDT, ZENUSDT, RSRUSDT, GALAUSDT, QTUMUSDT, DGBUSDT, YFIUSDT

Phase 2 cells (inactive until their own Coen-gated commit): timeframes 1h, 4h, 12h on the same assets

Phase 3 cells (inactive until their own Coen-gated commit): timeframes 15m, 30m on the same assets

The assets are listed in manifest order, and the same 76 are used in every phase. Phase 1 is active from the registry entry of this note. Phase 2 and phase 3 are not active at this entry: each is activated only by its own commit, which Coen decides. The grid is 76 assets by 6 timeframes, 456 cells in all, and 76 of them are active now. A phase 2 or phase 3 cell whose own first bar falls after 2022-12-31 is excluded when its phase is activated and is named in that phase's note; an exclusion never adds a cell.

THE EXCLUDED ASSETS. Each is the ticker followed by USDT. The first bar is the date of its first daily bar, first_1d_utc in data/crypto_universe_manifest.json. Ten have a first bar in 2024 and fourteen have one between 2023-03-17 and 2023-12-15. All 24 fall after 2022-12-31.

Excluded assets (24, not swept): ENA first bar 2024-04-02, ETHFI first bar 2024-03-18, JUP first bar 2024-01-31, PYTH first bar 2024-02-02, RENDER first bar 2024-07-26, STRK first bar 2024-02-20, TAO first bar 2024-04-11, WIF first bar 2024-03-05, ZK first bar 2024-06-17, ZRO first bar 2024-06-20, GAS first bar 2023-03-17, GLM first bar 2023-03-17, PROM first bar 2023-03-17, ARB first bar 2023-03-23, SUI first bar 2023-05-03, FLOKI first bar 2023-05-05, PEPE first bar 2023-05-05, PENDLE first bar 2023-07-03, WLD first bar 2023-07-24, SEI first bar 2023-08-15, TIA first bar 2023-10-31, ORDI first bar 2023-11-07, JTO first bar 2023-12-07, BONK first bar 2023-12-15

WHAT IS FIXED AND WHAT IS OPEN. The set of cells is fixed by this note. Only the timing of phases 2 and 3 is open. Nothing outside this grid can be added: not an asset, not a timeframe, not one of the 24 excluded assets, and not a cell of an asset that listed later. A pair that is delisted or halted is RETIRED by a new note that names it. A retirement never adds a cell. Every strategy registered on the retired pair stays on the chain.

THE POOLED PATH IS RETIRED. From this entry on no new pooled BTCUSD+ETHUSD spec is proposed. Every pooled strategy registered before this entry stays on the chain and re-simulates. Nothing about them is re-judged.

WHAT COUNTS. Each cell is its own counted trial. Activating a phase adds its cells to what is searched. More registrations at a fixed bar is arithmetic about the denominator, never evidence of edge.

payload.claim: MYR Group (MYRG), despite strong revenue growth, a 6.8% EBITDA margin, and net cash, was predicted to be vulnerable to downside because it traded at an elevated valuation of 23.4x EV/EBITDA and 29.1x forward P/E, with risk amplified if project timing slipped or the Valley acquisition took longer to integrate than expected.
payload.quote: I rated MYR Group a Sell because I thought the stock was already pricing in a lot of good news: strong revenue growth, a 6.8% EBITDA margin, and net cash, but also a valuation of 23.4x EV/EBITDA and 29.1x forward P/E. My view was that the downside case was easier to trigger than the upside case, especially if project timing slipped or the Valley acquisition took longer to integrate than expected.

source.title: The Scorecard: 3 Month Update: MYRG Sell — Correct so far

testability.notes: Qualitative execution-risk factors (project timing, acquisition integration) are harder to quantify with standard market data than the valuation multiples.

payload.claim: Shorting MYRG from its entry price of $391.51 on 2026-07-17 to $280.16 on 2026-10-16 would have returned 28.4%, consistent with the original Sell thesis based on valuation concerns.
payload.quote: Over this tracking window, following the Sell would have earned 28.4%, which means the short case has worked. MYRG has fallen from 391.51 to 280.16, so the market has not rewarded the valuation multiple I was worried about.

source.title: The Scorecard: 3 Month Update: MYRG Sell — Correct so far

data_required: MYRG daily closing price history from 2026-07-17 to 2026-10-16

payload.claim: SDGR was overvalued relative to its cash generation profile, as evidenced by a 56.9% gross margin combined with operating cash flow of -$126.9M TTM, an EV/Revenue multiple of 3.9x, and a P/S multiple of 5.1x, which was the basis for a Sell rating.
payload.quote: I argued that SDGR was still priced for growth that its cash generation had not earned, even though the platform itself looked solid. My sell case leaned on the gap between a healthy 56.9% gross margin and the much weaker cash profile, especially operating cash flow of -$126.9M TTM and a valuation of 3.9x EV/Revenue and 5.1x P/S.

source.title: The Scorecard: 2 Month Update: SDGR Sell — Incorrect so far

data_required: SDGR EV/Revenue and P/S historical multiples
testability.notes: Single-name case study; generalizable version would require screening a broader universe for similar margin/cash-flow/valuation profiles.

payload.claim: The sell thesis on SDGR would be invalidated (warranting a more constructive view) if SDGR's free cash flow turned positive and its revenue growth rate re-accelerated.
payload.quote: I also said I would only get more constructive if free cash flow turned positive and revenue growth re-accelerated.

source.title: The Scorecard: 2 Month Update: SDGR Sell — Incorrect so far

data_required: SDGR free cash flow by quarter
SDGR revenue growth rate by quarter
SDGR stock price around FCF/growth inflection points

payload.claim: Continued price advances in SDGR while its peer group remains mixed would further weaken the view that SDGR's valuation was detached from its fundamentals.
payload.quote: If SDGR keeps advancing while peers remain mixed, that would further weaken my view that the valuation was detached from fundamentals.

source.locator: What Could Still Prove Me Wrong section
source.title: The Scorecard: 2 Month Update: SDGR Sell — Incorrect so far

testability.notes: Peer group identity left as generic back-reference since the quote itself does not name the peers.
